title: YouTube / Video Platform
oneLine: Upload once to durable object storage, run an asynchronous transcoding DAG, package multiple renditions, and stream segments through a CDN with adaptive bitrate.
opening: I would split upload, processing, metadata, and playback. The client creates a video record and receives a multipart/resumable upload session to object storage. Completion emits an event into a transcoding DAG: validate and scan, split into chunks, encode multiple codecs/resolutions/bitrates, generate thumbnails/captions, package HLS or DASH manifests and segments, then publish atomically. Metadata lives in a relational or document store; large media stays in object storage. Playback fetches metadata and an authorized manifest, then the player selects bitrate adaptively while segments are served from CDN. Popular content is edge-cached; long-tail and originals use tiered storage. Every processing task is idempotent, retryable, and versioned so a new codec can be backfilled safely.
ask: Upload and on-demand playback only, or live streaming too?
How quickly must a video become playable?
What are upload volume, watch traffic, retention, and regional constraints?
scale: Egress dominates cost: watch minutes × delivered bitrate is more important than metadata QPS.
Transcoding expands one original into multiple renditions; estimate compute and storage multiplier by ladder.
Chunked segments allow CDN caching and adaptive bitrate without downloading a whole file.

decisions.default: Direct multipart upload to object storage using short-lived signed URLs.
decisions.why: Application servers avoid proxying multi-GB payloads and resumability is native.
decisions.switch: Proxy only when content inspection must occur before any bytes reach storage.

decisions.default: Idempotent DAG of small tasks with durable state.
decisions.why: Different renditions can run in parallel and failed work can resume selectively.
decisions.switch: Single managed transcoding job for simpler moderate-scale deployments.

decisions.default: Segmented adaptive HLS/DASH with a bitrate ladder.
decisions.why: The client adapts to bandwidth and CDN caches standard objects.
decisions.switch: Low-latency live protocols need shorter segments/chunks and different delivery trade-offs.

decisions.default: Provide a widely compatible baseline plus newer efficient codec for capable devices.
decisions.why: Storage/transcode cost trades against ongoing egress savings and device support.
decisions.switch: Per-title or per-shot encoding for high-volume content where bandwidth savings justify compute complexity.

deepDives.title: Transcoding DAG
points: Preprocessor validates container, extracts metadata, scans, and splits work.
Scheduler assigns CPU/GPU workers by codec/resolution and tracks task state.
Publish only after required renditions and manifest pass validation; optional renditions can arrive later.

deepDives.title: Playback quality
points: Use origin shield and regional CDN to protect storage.
Player adapts from throughput/buffer; collect startup time, rebuffers, bitrate switches, and errors.
Signed manifests/URLs and DRM keys enforce access without putting authorization on every segment request.

deepDives.title: Cost control
points: Tier originals and unpopular renditions to colder storage.
Encode only ladders demanded by device/content profile.
Deduplicate retries and use spot/preemptible capacity for non-urgent backfills.

failures.response: Multipart session, per-part checksum, resume token, and idempotent completion.
Retry only that DAG node, preserve intermediate artifacts, DLQ after classified attempts, and surface processing state.
Origin shield, request coalescing, pre-warm launch content, and bounded origin concurrency.
Automated media validation, immutable versioned manifests, canary playback, and rollback to previous package.

questions.q: Why not stream the original file?
questions.a: Devices and networks differ. Multiple segmented renditions enable adaptive bitrate, fast seek, CDN caching, and compatible codecs, while protecting the large origin object.
The server creates an upload session; the client sends numbered parts directly to object storage with checksums; completion atomically assembles the object and emits one processing event.

questions.q: How do you support a new codec?
questions.a: Version the processing graph and run an asynchronous backfill prioritized by watch volume. Publish the new rendition into a new manifest version without rewriting the original.

questions.q: What is the source of truth during processing?
questions.a: A durable video-processing state machine plus immutable object artifacts. Queue delivery is only a trigger; task completion is recorded idempotently in durable state.

mistakes: Sending large uploads through application servers
Treating transcoding as one unrecoverable job
Publishing a manifest before required artifacts are valid
seniorSignal: Separate the control plane from the byte path. Discuss resumability, atomic publication, idempotent DAG execution, QoE telemetry, origin protection, and cost per watched minute.
implementation: Object storage multipart upload + signed URLs
Kafka/SQS trigger and workflow/DAG orchestrator with CPU/GPU workers
HLS/DASH manifests, CDN, origin shield, signed playback URLs
Relational metadata/state plus immutable media artifacts
